# Gospel of Thomas, Saying 64 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Nag Hammadi Codex II, p. 47-48 | **Source Image:** source-texts/coptic/GTH_064_page_001.jpg

---

## Saying 64

**1** Jesus said: "A man had guests, and when he had prepared the dinner, he sent his servant to invite the guests.

**2** He went to the first one and said to him: 'My master invites you.' He said: 'I have money with some merchants. They are coming to me this evening. I must go and give them my orders. I ask to be excused from the dinner.'

**3** He went to another and said to him: 'My master has invited you.' He said: 'I have bought a house and am required there for a day. I will have no time.'

**4** He went to another and said to him: 'My master invites you.' He said: 'A friend of mine is to be married, and I am to arrange the dinner. I shall not be able to come. I ask to be excused from the dinner.'

**5** He went to another and said to him: 'My master invites you.' He said: 'I have bought a farm. I am going to collect the rent. I shall not be able to come. I ask to be excused.'

**6** The servant came back and said to his master: 'Those whom you invited to the dinner have asked to be excused.'

**7** The master said to his servant: 'Go outside to the streets and bring back those whom you happen to meet, so that they may dine.'

**8** Businessmen and merchants will not enter the places of my Father."

---

**Consensus Notes (SOPHIA):**

**Text:** Thomas's version of the Great Banquet parable (cf. Luke 14, Matt 22) has four excused guests, all with commercial or social motives. There is no violence, no burning of cities.

**"Places of my Father"** — *topos*: LOGOS/EMET preserve "places"; PNEUMA's "domain" is interpretively richer but moves away from the Coptic *topos*.

**"Businessmen and merchants"** — EMET preserves both Coptic terms: *mpole* and *emporos* — traders and merchants. Both terms retained to preserve the double condemnation of commercial preoccupation.

**Theological Note:** The final condemnatory line is unique to Thomas: commercial preoccupation disqualifies entry into the Father's domain. The parable moves from narrative to theological decree.

**Synoptic Parallels:** Luke 14:16-24; Matt 22:1-14. Thomas's version lacks the Lukan social ethic (inviting the poor) and the Matthean violence (king's army). The focus is purely on the commercial excuses and their spiritual consequences.
